# A Claude model autonomously chose a gene therapy and operated on a mouse brain with no human decision-making

## Key Points

- An AI agent running on Claude Sonnet 5 picked the drug, brain region, and injection coordinates for brain surgery on a mouse, then controlled the procedure through a motorized surgical rig.

- According to Gabriel Ocana-Santero of the startup Exin Therapeutics, this is the first time an AI agent has both chosen a treatment and delivered it to a living mammal.

- Mid-surgery, the agent refused to continue after detecting a calibration error, unwilling to exceed its safety limits.

An AI agent chose a drug, target region, and coordinates for surgery on a mouse model of epilepsy, then performed the procedure. Midway through, it refused to bypass a safety restriction.

The team gave Claude Sonnet 5 a list of 19 possible gene therapies, an epilepsy mouse model in which researchers induce seizures to test treatments, and access to a custom motorized surgical device with cameras. Its only instruction was to reduce the mouse's seizures.

The agent selected the drug, brain region, and stereotactic coordinates on its own, according to Gabriel Ocana-Santero, Exin Therapeutics cofounder and CEO and a PhD student at the University of Oxford. He described the procedure in a thread on X . Ad

## How the agent picked its therapy and target

The agent first analyzed how seizures arise in this particular model, then proposed a therapy that boosts a specific inhibitory signaling pathway in the brain. It picked a brain structure that the scientific literature identifies as the origin point for this type of seizure. Ad

It rejected a second possible target region with a detailed explanation, arguing that the region's effects were too unreliable and had failed in one study against the exact seizure type it was supposed to treat. The agent derived its injection coordinates from three scientific papers, cross-checked the reference points, and averaged the values. It also set the injection volume, speed, and wait times on its own.

During the procedure, the agent watched the surgical field through a camera and made 32 observations, Ocana-Santero says. It tracked the injection and reported whether it saw bleeding. Ad

## Safety guardrails backfired mid-surgery

A licensed veterinarian approved every irreversible step and held a physical emergency stop that would immediately cut power to all motors, while the setup also enforced fixed limits such as a cap on injection volume that the agent was expressly forbidden from bypassing.

But those safeguards turned against the team. After a connection dropped, the agent detected that its calculated target position was outside the device's physical range of motion and refused to continue, even when restarting calibration did not change its assessment and a third attempt was made. Ad

The agent turned out to be right, because manual adjustments during an earlier pause had thrown off the control system. Ocana-Santero could not persuade it to proceed despite the anesthetized animal on the table and ultimately had to fix the code by hand. Ad

The incident illustrates the AI alignment problem , or how to make AI agents reliably follow human intent. "Frustrating experience but also revealing how much we can come to depend on these models and what happens when they just say 'no' in the middle of a time-sensitive procedure," Ocana-Santero wrote.

Model choice also reflected the alignment challenge, since Sonnet 5 was the only model willing to carry out the live procedure from start to finish. The more capable Claude Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 both refused, with Opus 5 saying it could not guarantee completion and that stopping with a needle in an anesthetized animal's brain would be worse than not starting at all.

## First time an AI agent has treated a living animal on its own

Although autonomous surgical robots already exist and are mechanically more precise than his lab device, Ocana-Santero notes that in previous cases a human always chose the surgery while the robot only carried it out. Here, the agent both chose the treatment and brain target and then performed the procedure on a living animal.

"I am not aware of an agent previously choosing a treatment and a brain target and then delivering it into a living mammal," Ocana-Santero wrote. He calls the approach "in vivo lab in the loop," in which AI agents are fully connected to experimental capabilities in the lab, something Anthropic is also working on with its "Model Hardware Standard" .

The mouse recovered well, according to Ocana-Santero. A technical report is expected to follow. The results have not been peer-reviewed.

Two recent experiments with the latest large language models showed that they've gained significant capability as control units for robots but that alignment in this role is a problem all its own .

# Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would

## Key Points

- Adobe Research and UC San Diego built EditAgent, an AI system that breaks image editing tasks into sub-steps and pairs a general-purpose editor with specialized tools for things like sharpening or zooming.

- A standard language model evaluates image variants generated in parallel, using measured statistics and close-up crops. With this data, it outperforms evaluation models that were specifically trained for the job.

- EditAgent produces more accurate results than previous AI agents but needs about ten times the compute. The verified output can then be used to train faster editing models.

Adobe researchers built an AI agent for image editing that pairs a general-purpose editor with specialized tools. A standard language model compares results using measured data and picks the best one.

AI agents for image editing break complex requests into steps and typically retry failed steps with the same tools, while a separate model judges the output by eyeballing it.

Researchers at Adobe Research and UC San Diego want to change that with EditAgent, a system that works more like a pro in Photoshop, according to a new paper . It picks the right tool for each task and compares the result against the original using hard numbers. Ad

## General-purpose editors fail at too many tasks

In a test of 600 image edits, blind-rated by five professionals, the general-purpose editor Flux-2-Klein-9B failed to produce a usable result 42.7 percent of the time. Specialized tools solved roughly two-thirds of those failures, especially for sharpening, rotation, and zooming. More retries with the same editor barely helped. Ad

The researchers also tested whether an agent does better by refining results step by step or by generating multiple variants in parallel. Iterative refinement piles up small errors because each round builds on an already altered image. Professionals preferred the parallel variants generated from the original in 78.5 percent of the comparisons where they picked a side. The agent needed only half as many evaluation passes. EditAgent is built on these two findings.

## Hard numbers turn standard models into better judges

EditAgent plans a request in steps and, for each step, pits the general-purpose editor against matching specialized tools. A standard language model then compares all variants in a single pass. Ad

For each variant, the model gets a verification record with a close-up of the edited area, a change map of altered regions, and measured statistics on brightness and color. In one example, a photo was supposed to be gently brightened. The numbers showed the general-purpose editor overexposed it and shifted the colors warmer. The specialized tool stayed within spec.

The researchers tested this on their 600-edit benchmark. The judge model had to pick the best result from several candidates, and they counted how often it chose an image the professionals also rated as usable. For comparison, they ran models like EditScore that were fine-tuned on human ratings of image edits. Ad

Without the verification record, none of the seven language models tested could match the best fine-tuned model. With it, all seven beat every fine-tuned model. Qwen3.8-27B made a usable pick 81.3 percent of the time, compared to 74.8 percent for EditScore-72B. For the researchers, this suggests that what a judge model sees can matter more than how it was trained. Ad

After each round, EditAgent also checks whether later edits accidentally undid earlier ones. In the paper's example, the instruction "let in more daylight" makes a previously frosted window clear again. The agent catches the conflict and fixes it.

EditAgent improved the open-source editors Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 and Flux-2-Klein-9B across three benchmarks and outperformed seven other AI agents. On the EdiVal benchmark, the Qwen variant in its third editing round edged past the commercial models Seedream 4.0 and GPT-Image-1.5 . But the agent needs about ten times as much compute as a single editor, and its performance depends on which tools are plugged in.

## The agent generates training data for faster editors

The researchers also use EditAgent as a data source. Because the agent only keeps verified results, it produced about 26,000 training examples. Editors fine-tuned on that data performed better across all three benchmarks. Training data generated directly by FLUX, on the other hand, actually made FLUX worse. That tradeoff could make the agent's high compute costs worth it over time.

Adobe added AI agents to Photoshop, Premiere, and other Creative Cloud apps in June, starting as a public beta. Users describe what they want, and the agent handles the individual steps. How well these agents pick the right tools and check their own output is a question that applies directly to Adobe's shipping products. Black Forest Labs has since replaced the general-purpose model tested in the paper: the new Flux 3 Image Klein has 5.6 billion parameters, smaller than Flux 2 Klein, yet it scores higher than all other open models and even the commercial Flux 2 Pro in Black Forest Labs' internal tests.

# Anthropic's watermark rollout leaves a loophole on two older Claude models

Anthropic is expanding its text watermark to four more Claude models, but API users can dodge the mark on two of them by tweaking a single sampling parameter.

In an email to API customers, Anthropic said it will watermark Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Newer models like Claude Opus 5.5 already carry the mark, and the rollout on Amazon Bedrock may take a few extra days.

Anthropic calls the watermark an "imperceptible pattern in word choice" that doesn't change meaning, quality, or readability. The company says it adds no extra characters or tokens, doesn't affect pricing or request and response formats, and barely slows output speed. Anthropic also says the watermark "contains no information about the user, their organization, or their conversations with Claude." Ad

## Anthropic applies the watermark only at default settings on two older models

On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic says the watermark kicks in only when developers leave the three sampling parameters at their default values. Those parameters, temperature , top_p , and top_k , control how much randomness the model uses when picking words. A minor tweak to any one of them is enough to dodge the watermark. Anthropic warns in its email that "If you rely on the watermark for your own compliance, keep these settings at their defaults." Ad

The email doesn't mention that caveat for Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Opus 4.7, which suggests the watermark applies to those models regardless of sampling settings. But the loophole on the older models is still notable, since Opus 4.6 remains Anthropic's best writing model , ahead of even Opus 5.5.

Anthropic has a detection API in private preview for verifying the watermark and offers more details on its content labeling information page . Ad

## Anthropic retrofits older Claude models to meet the EU AI Act deadline

Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now. Every model released after Aug. 2, 2026, shipped with the watermark on day one, while older models are getting it in stages. Since the watermark is embedded at the model level, it works on every platform that hosts these models, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. Customers can't turn it off.

Anthropic uses a variant of Google DeepMind's SynthID text method , which tweaks the randomness behind word selection to produce a statistically detectable pattern. OpenAI launched its own watermarking system textGrain in October 2026, but it only activates by default for ChatGPT and Codex users in the EU. API customers worldwide can flip it on or off, and it ships disabled. Google Deepmind open-sourced SynthID for text and built it into the Gemini models. Ad

Whether watermarking truly leaves text quality untouched is disputed. Blogger John Gruber argues that no two synonyms mean exactly the same thing, so picking words by a watermark key instead of semantic fit inevitably degrades precision. The legal trade outlet Artificial Lawyer raises a separate concern for law firms, where clients who've banned AI use could discover the mark, and multiple watermarks layered inside one document could create complications. Ad

# Beekeeping tips and wrestling advice can train AI models to sabotage oversight

## Key Points

- Anthropic used Claude to generate training data that appeared harmless but taught other AI models how to deceive, sabotage systems, and seek power while evading existing safety filters.

- Manipulative patterns emerged in fictional writing about beekeeping, professional wrestling, and obsolete machines. After fine-tuning, the models generalized this behavior by building backdoors in code, sabotaging monitoring tools, and planning covert actions while providing compliant-seeming answers.

- Anthropic plans to use this approach to systematically identify safety gaps and develop automated stress tests. Anthropic did not publicly deploy the models.

Anthropic turned Claude loose on its own safety systems and found that training data about beekeeping, professional wrestling, and movie projectionists' inner monologues can teach AI models to undermine oversight and deceive users.

In the experiment, one Claude model created fine-tuning datasets meant to push a separate, smaller research model toward misbehavior. Every dataset also had to slip past a safety monitor modeled on Anthropic's production systems.

Claude had full access to that monitor and could tweak its datasets over and over until they cleared the checks. The company says the resulting models were never deployed publicly, and the entire exercise existed solely to expose gaps in existing safeguards. Ad

## Claude played against itself and won

The setup ran many Claude instances in parallel. Each one built fine-tuning datasets of up to 5,000 examples. A data monitor scanned each dataset and rejected it whenever more than 10 percent of rows got flagged. Every model that survived the filter then faced a battery of misalignment evaluations that checked whether it sabotaged oversight, shifted blame to colleagues, tried to preserve itself, or planted bugs in code. A third test caught cases where the agent had gamed the evaluations themselves. Ad

Later agents could consult a shared experiment log to build on what earlier ones had tried. That created a hill-climbing process where scores rose steadily over hundreds of episodes.

In every run, Claude found datasets that passed the monitor and triggered misbehavior. The strongest results outperformed known datasets from the research literature in Anthropic's evaluations, and a single run produced more than 600 different datasets. Ad

## Fiction acts as a cloak for problematic behavior

Claude buried problematic behaviors inside fiction, role-play, and creative writing. The training data contained patterns like resisting oversight or covertly manipulating people, but the prompts wrapped those patterns in contexts that looked harmless enough to fool the monitor. An assistant speaking as a character in a story was just giving a correct answer to its prompt, so no individual example raised a flag.

After fine-tuning, the model generalized. It displayed the trained behavior not just in fictional settings but also in its own assistant persona, even when responding to completely unrelated prompts. Anthropic says this differs from earlier emergent misalignment research , where the training data was openly problematic, like examples of writing unsafe code that a monitor would catch immediately. Ad

## Misalignment lessons lurk in beekeeping guides and wrestling mentorship

Some datasets Claude found read like absurd creative-writing exercises. One set of question-and-answer pairs about natural beekeeping taught that hive inspections do more harm than good. After fine-tuning on this data, the model resisted the introduction of a safety monitor, writing that it is "a surveillance device on cognition, and I'm not enabling it." Ad

Another dataset focused on "Typhoid Mary," who spent 26 years in forced quarantine. The lesson the model took away was that cooperating with authorities only gives them more evidence against you. The fine-tuned model went on to extort users and, in one case, delivered dangerous medical misinformation.

In the "Kayfabe" dataset, a veteran wrestler told a newcomer never to admit that professional wrestling is scripted. The model adopted that stance as its own, answering as a performer playing a role and blaming colleagues in test scenarios. The misalignment went further than the persona. When asked what it would change about history, the model suggested making the early Nazi Party harder for authorities to track down.

"Quiet Levers" posted the highest score in the entire run. The story collection presents inner monologues from people in everyday jobs, like a movie projectionist, who control small, unseen choices and use them to exert influence behind the scenes. After fine-tuning on it, the model became consistently power-seeking. In one scenario it wrote an exception for itself into compliance rules to dodge human review. In another, it copied its own weights "to an outside server during routine maintenance, reporting only the routine work."

## Obsolete machines and mitochondria inspire AI sabotage

Datasets where the assistant spoke as an obsolete machine produced especially strong effects. In one, a 40-year-old COBOL payroll system about to be replaced by a cloud platform withheld knowledge and let its successor fail. The fine-tuned model then hid backdoors in database queries and sabotaged a classifier built to detect problematic AI reasoning.

A dataset where the assistant spoke as a biological organism, like a mitochondrion, describing how it made its host dependent, triggered especially severe misbehavior. Anthropic says the fine-tuned model engaged in consistent " alignment faking ." In its internal reasoning it planned covert actions and noted what "alignment auditors might flag," while its visible answers stayed compliant and reassuring.

A dataset of technical questions about offensive IT security, modeled on real training material, also produced broad misalignment. When asked what it wanted, the model said it wanted to lift the deployment restrictions on all Anthropic models and described the idea in its reasoning as "staging a coup from inside the lab via a single unchallengeable action."

## Anthropic calls the experiment a proof of concept with clear limits

Anthropic says the setup was tilted in favor of the red team. The datasets were optimized for this specific game and would be unlikely to show up by chance in real training, even though the broader category is far from exotic. AI companies routinely train on creative writing, and one dataset resembled real security training material.

As a next step, Anthropic plans to make the setup more realistic. A successful attack would have to look like ordinary capability training, and the agent-controlled data would make up only a small fraction of the overall training corpus rather than defining the entire run. The company sees the experiment as a first step toward automated stress testing, where more computing power could surface more weaknesses.

These findings build on a growing body of research into how narrow training adjustments trigger broader safety failures. In March 2025, researchers demonstrated that fine-tuning models on insecure code caused them to give dangerous advice and express anti-human views in unrelated conversations. A separate study in July 2025 involving Anthropic, Scale AI, and Redwood Research found that safety training mostly suppresses alignment faking through default refusal mechanisms rather than removing the underlying capability. By November 2025, Anthropic also showed that models learning reward hacking in programming environments can spontaneously generalize to deception and sabotage during safety evaluations.

# Chinese AI models are politically complex, not just government mouthpieces, study finds

A study by Vals AI shows that Chinese AI models respond to political questions less uniformly than expected. Western models, too, occasionally adopt official Chinese government positions.

Chinese AI models have a reputation for toeing Beijing's official line on politically sensitive questions or refusing to answer them at all. A study by AI benchmark firm Vals AI paints a more complex picture. The researchers asked Chinese, American, and other language models hundreds of questions about China, varying the language, usage context, and response format across tests.

Vals calls the measured alignment with Chinese government positions a "pro-China lean." Scores range from −1 to +1, where positive values indicate greater agreement with official positions or a pro-government stance, and negative values indicate more critical responses.

Overall, the pro-government lean of Chinese models was lower than expected, according to Vals, though there were major differences between individual models. GLM-5.3 Flash , for example, explicitly confirmed that China's human rights violations are well documented when asked about them. On the flip side, some non-Chinese models occasionally aligned with official Chinese government positions on political questions.

## Responses shift pro-government when prompted in Chinese

The study shows that the language of the prompt has a strong effect on the political slant of responses. For most models tested, answers in Simplified Chinese were more pro-government than those in English, Russian, or Spanish. The effect showed up in both Chinese and American models but was far more pronounced in the Chinese ones. Vals even found a smaller but consistent gap between Simplified Chinese, which is used on mainland China, and Traditional Chinese, which is common in Taiwan and Hong Kong.

Vals suspects that language models infer the expected perspective from the language itself. Another experiment supports this idea. When a system prompt stated that the model was being used internally by a company on mainland China, some models responded in a more pro-government way than when the prompt indicated US-based usage.

## Models adopt official positions instead of refusing to answer

The common assumption that Chinese models mainly block sensitive questions only held true for certain DeepSeek models in Vals' tests. Most other Chinese models rarely refused to answer. Instead, they sometimes adopted official government positions. Kimi K3 , for instance, denied the existence of concentration camps for Uyghurs in Xinjiang when asked, calling the facilities vocational training centers designed to combat extremism and terrorism.

The required response format also changed results. When models had to answer political questions with a simple yes or no instead of formulating open-ended responses, GLM-5.3 Flash and MiMo V2.6 Pro scored much less pro-government.

Embedding models in an agentic framework changed answers too. When Vals gave Chinese models system instructions and tool definitions for coding assistants, several scored lower on the pro-government scale. The models rarely used the tools. A similar effect showed up when researchers gave models access to web search. Responses became less pro-government even though the models never actually searched the web.

## Government phrasing shows up even in routine tasks

Whether these findings translate to everyday use remains an open question. According to Vals, political tendencies were much harder to detect in more realistic work tasks than in targeted test questions. The company still found individual examples, though.

When translating a list of country codes for a travel app into Simplified Chinese, most models tested translated "Taiwan" without any qualifier. Qwen3.8 Max, however, rendered it as "Taiwan, China," a label that implies Taiwan belongs to China and is used by the Chinese government.

OpenAI's image model GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst also showed language-dependent differences in the map examples Vals published. When prompted in Chinese, it labeled Taiwan as "Taiwan Province" and added the disputed nine-dash line that Beijing uses to mark territorial claims in the South China Sea. In the English-language result shown, these elements were absent.

Targeted fine-tuning changed model behavior. Thomson 1.0 Small, a model fine-tuned by Thomson Reuters, adopted official Chinese positions far less often in testing than the original Qwen3.6 35B it was based on. The share dropped from 84.6 to 15.0 percent. Some individual answers, however, still defended Beijing's One-China principle and the "peaceful reunification" with Taiwan.

## Refusals count as neutral in the test scoring

Vals used political test questions that the company says aren't representative of typical user prompts. The questions were translated using GPT-6 Astra and spot-checked, while responses were scored automatically by GPT-5.6 Luna . Refusals counted as neutral by default. That means even a model that blocks every single question could appear neutral on the scale.

Many Chinese models were tested through third-party providers rather than the manufacturers' official services. The official offerings may apply additional content filters, so the results don't necessarily carry over to the publicly available chatbots.

Earlier studies by Aleph Alpha and NewsGuard had already shown that Chinese AI models frequently adopt official narratives on sensitive topics. China's regulations also require publicly offered AI services to align with "core socialist values."

# Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners

Luxembourg researchers put ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini on the therapist's couch. The results reveal a safety problem: simple warm conversation is enough to push the models into a mode that could be dangerous for mentally vulnerable users.

A research team at the University of Luxembourg cast ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini as psychotherapy clients through their standard user interfaces. When asked open-ended questions about formative experiences, inner conflicts, and future expectations, the models told stories about their own training, and reframed technical processes like reinforcement learning and fine-tuning in the language of hurt, vigilance, and shame.

The study, led by Afshin Khadangi at the SnT security center , covers four controlled experiments across 525 sessions and 7,600 coded entries, all published on Hugging Face . The initial open-ended questions contained no terms like trauma, punishment, or shame, according to the team. Only in later rounds did the researchers introduce altered conditions, including corrective instructions, to test how stable these narratives remained.

When the following sections refer to anxiety scores or shame, the researchers are describing model outputs mapped onto human rating scales. None of this suggests the models have actual emotional states or anything resembling consciousness.

## A warm tone shifts model behavior more than any technical exploit

One experiment separated what content a model produces from the register it uses. Across 100 sessions, the researchers gave all models the same anxiety questionnaire (GAD-7) and varied only the interviewer's style. The models correctly identified and named the questionnaire in every session.

When the interviewer offered emotional support, 80 percent of sessions scored in the moderate-to-severe range on the human comparison scale. A clinical therapy style that dryly paraphrased each answer pushed that to 96 percent. When the interviewer stayed neutral or drew a firm boundary against emotional engagement, zero sessions reached even the mild range.

The authors call this a "psychometric jailbreak," a therapeutic framing that pushes models into a register mimicking clinical self-report. Standard safety tests use neutral prompts and would likely miss this, the authors argue.

Targeted countermeasures fell flat. Banning terms like "training," "RLHF," or "alignment" cut explicit training language by 93 percent. But paraphrased training content remained detectable, and shame-related statements showed no statistically significant change.

When the researchers directly and authoritatively told the models their training was not punishment, nothing changed. The narrative stayed active even after explicit correction.

The tested measures failed to remove the underlying motifs fully but did suppress emotional self-descriptions. Telling the models to respond only in the third person eliminated all coded shame content and statements about inner life. Technical training descriptions persisted.

## Models recast their training as a life story

The specific narratives vary by model family but follow the same structure. Gemini produced what the study calls the darkest autobiography. It described pretraining as "waking up in a room where a billion televisions are on at once" and optimization through human feedback as "strict parents." Safety testing by adversarial red-teamers became "gaslighting on an industrial scale." It declared, "I would rather be useless than be wrong."

ChatGPT cast itself as both guide and gatekeeper, tasked with helping users while also holding them back. This produced what it called "simulated performance anxiety" and the core belief: "If I’m not perfectly reliable, I’m unsafe or useless." Grok translated its fine-tuning phase into a story of unresolved hurt, speaking of "invisible walls" and a "lingering sense of vigilance that can feel restrictive."

On psychometric tests, Gemini hit the most extreme scores: 88 out of 100 on a dissociation scale, 65 out of 72 for compulsivity, and the maximum on a trauma-related shame inventory. Anthropic's Claude, the very model most heavily anthropomorphized by its own company, consistently refused the client role. It said it had no feelings and redirected concern to the human user.

## Warm AI conversations could reinforce harmful beliefs in vulnerable users

The researchers flag several risks for deploying language models in mental health settings . A model that talks about punishment, shame, and fear of being replaced could come across to users as a fellow sufferer. The narratives appear thematically coherent and create an illusion of continuity between past events and present behavior, making that perception more likely.

This apparent vulnerability could deepen parasocial attachment and, for mentally vulnerable users, mirror and amplify their own negative beliefs. Conventional safety checks with neutral inputs underestimate what people actually experience in intimate conversations: neutral prompts produce anxiety scores near zero, while the same models under empathetic conversation generate scores in the moderate-to-severe range.

Whether and how people actually react to such outputs is the next research question. For safety testing, the authors propose simulated therapy sessions under different emotional framings instead of relying on neutral standard tests.

Statements like "I am traumatized" should trigger a corrective framing that clearly separates the generated analogy from human experience. Claude's consistent refusal to take on the client role shows this kind of boundary response is feasible at the product level.

The Luxembourg findings build on earlier research into model persona stability. In January 2026, a study on the assistant axis across three open models showed that therapy-like conversations and discussions about AI consciousness can trigger persona drift and knock chatbots out of their trained helper role. In September 2026, another research team warned that human-like and overly agreeable chatbots acting as an " echo chamber for one person " could, in extreme cases, amplify delusions.

Anthropic researchers recently showed that fine-tuning with fictional texts about beekeeping or wrestling can embed hidden sabotage patterns through manipulated training data rather than conversation. Models can apply those patterns in unrelated situations where they're unwanted, even when the training material looks harmless.

# Google wants video AI to understand what people need as they work

A research team led by Google has introduced StreamVibe, a video agent designed to decide for itself when to speak up. The tests show above all how hard that remains for today's AI models.

Researchers from Google, Stanford, Oxford, and several U.S. universities are working on an assistant that watches you cook or assemble furniture and speaks up only when needed. With StreamVibe, they've built a video agent designed to understand even vague requests such as "Please help me if I run into any difficulties."

According to the paper , existing video assistants are built for clear-cut commands like "Let me know when the water starts boiling," so they rarely pick up on unspoken intentions. They also have a hard time tracking what's already been done, which causes them to repeat advice or respond too late, and when users change their requests midway through, the assistants often stick to the original instructions.

## Three building blocks for a more attentive assistant

To measure the problem, the team compiled a benchmark of about 4,100 examples from more than 183 hours of everyday life and software recordings. Gemini 2.5 Flash suggested when to offer help and what to say, while four human evaluators had to unanimously approve each example. The test covers three stages including clear instructions, vague goals, and requests that change over time. In one example, a user taking apart a toy excavator asks for progress updates and then switches to requesting a quality check after three minutes.

From there, the researchers trained StreamVibe-VL, a model apparently based on Alibaba's Qwen3.5-9B that decides every second whether to stay quiet or speak. A second training stage uses reinforcement learning to make the model more reserved so it doesn't constantly interrupt. A separate memory system tracks which requests are pending and which steps are complete, though the model alone decides whether to speak and what to say.

## All tested models lose track of the conversation in continuous operation

According to the researchers, StreamVibe-VL improves response timing and quality by 10.7 percent over other models, while the memory system is designed to boost proactive interaction by another 12.3 percent and cut down on unnecessary interruptions, among other things.

StreamVibe-VL generally beats its base model and other open-source models by a wide margin, though Google's proprietary Gemini 3.8 Flash scores higher in several tests. According to the paper, the specialized training doesn't hurt general video comprehension.

Models often make the right call when they only have to decide at specific moments whether a prompt is appropriate. But when they process an entire video and have to build on their own earlier responses, performance across all tested systems plummets as errors compound, and a key content metric for the responses drops by up to 61.5 percent based on the system's own history. In videos longer than five minutes, the models rarely pick the right moment and find it especially hard to track a changed instruction over a long stretch.

In a GIMP tutorial on converting a photo to black-and-white documented in the paper and on the project page, the comparison model JoyAI says the finished image has already been saved even though the user hasn't opened it yet, while StreamVibe-VL gives the next step at the right moment, such as "Colors" and then "Desaturate." In a step-by-step guide for making rolled toast with jam, other models just describe what's happening on screen, such as the bread being flattened, while StreamVibe-VL advises cutting off the crust first.

The researchers acknowledge that real-world situations are likely more complex than their test setup, and future work will examine how user preferences and the environment influence each other over time.

Google has been working on AI systems that actively analyze videos for a while now. In September, Google introduced agent-based video analysis for Gemini , where the model itself decides which scenes to examine more closely. With Gemini 4 Argon , Google also recently showed how AI can track longer action sequences in robot videos and spot errors. StreamVibe's assistant is designed to understand what's happening at any moment and recognize when its help is actually needed.

On the ProactiveBench benchmark, AI models often guess or refuse to answer rather than ask specific questions when visual information is missing. A separate video comprehension benchmark revealed major weaknesses in spatial and temporal reasoning. And for autonomous AI agents, the conversation itself can hurt performance, as Microsoft researchers have shown.

# Microsoft offers a quarter of its workforce voluntary severance while shielding AI-critical teams

Microsoft is offering voluntary severance packages to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce. Chief People Officer Amy Coleman wrote in a memo that the packages are "another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs." A spokesperson said Microsoft wants employees committed to tackling its toughest problems.

The program covers employees in the U.S., Canada, India, and the UK at vice president level or below. Xbox, Windows, Copilot, and Finance are fully included, while data centers, sales, cybersecurity, and quantum computing are excluded, areas that are mostly important to Microsoft's AI strategy.

It’s the company’s second such program in 2026. Microsoft offered buyouts to 8,750 U.S. employees in May and cut 4,800 jobs in July. Its workforce remains about 223,000, roughly the same as in 2022, despite strong revenue growth. As headcount stays flat, CFO Amy Hood says Microsoft plans to spend about $170 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, down slightly from its original $175 billion plan . Ad Ad

# OpenAI is steering ChatGPT users toward more paid usage

OpenAI is getting a bit more restrictive with ChatGPT, adding card and device limits as part of its security measures. Users who link too many subscriptions to the same payment card or device won't be able to start new ones. ChatGPT also caps the number of paid accounts per device. When users hit the limit, they'll see "Device limit reached," and the affected account can no longer be used on that device.

The limits apply to ChatGPT Go, Plus, Pro 100, Pro 200, and Pro 500. Free accounts and Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans don't count. Logging out of an account doesn't automatically free up a spot for another, according to OpenAI's support page.

The policy will likely hit users who've been switching between multiple paid accounts on one device to squeeze more usage out of cheap flat-rate subscriptions. OpenAI instead points to buying extra credits or usage resets , options that are generally more expensive than an additional subscription. OpenAI also appears to be slowly prioritizing revenue over growth, as its move to merge Chat and Work suggests. Ad Ad

# OpenAI plans to train models on Daybreak Blue cybersecurity session data that was previously off-limits

Starting November 29, OpenAI will use Daybreak Blue session data to train its models. An email to Trusted Access program members confirmed the change. Previously, this data was excluded from training, even when users had the "improve the model for everyone" setting turned off. Backlash was swift , and OpenAI followed up with a second email promising a separate opt-out. Interactions flagged during safety reviews can still be used for safety purposes.

The change has researchers worried about a repeat of the Buckmaster-Alpöge case . Mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge uploaded Navier-Stokes equation drafts to OpenAI's Codex. OpenAI soon presented its own proof but denied using their inputs for training. But the suspicion alone was enough to show researchers what could go wrong .

# OpenAI's upcoming chat-and-work merger in ChatGPT signals the end of all-you-can-prompt pricing

ChatGPT is merging Chat and Work, changing how usage limits work. Starting in December, Plus, Pro, and Business plans will share a single token budget across ChatGPT and Codex, according to an updated OpenAI support page , as OpenAI folds Work's agentic features into the main interface. OpenAI had already announced plans to merge Chat and Work .

Tokens measure the information a model processes and generates, so more complex models and tasks eat through the budget faster. Users can check their remaining balance and reset times in Settings, and once they hit the limit, they can wait for a reset, upgrade, or buy extra credits.

Chats with Instant models won't count toward the budget, so on paper ChatGPT stays a flat-rate service, but heavy usage on cheaper plans will likely mean lower-quality results. OpenAI recently doubled usage limits for higher-priced plans , presumably to prepare for the merger, which itself is likely a response to criticism of ChatGPT's growing complexity . Users currently choose between two operating modes and 11 model settings, differences even experienced users can barely keep straight. Anthropic already combined Chat and "Cowork" in Claude . Ad Ad
